meta.title: Supervised, Unsupervised, and Reinforcement Learning
meta.thesis: Supervised, Unsupervised, and Reinforcement Learning is practical when learners can apply it to this concrete case: A product team must choose whether labels, clusters, or rewards match a new AI feature. By the end, they should be able to build or review learning-paradigm decision guide for support and operations tasks, measure labels, clusters, or rewards match a new AI feature. They do not need trivia about Supervised, Unsupervised, and Reinforcement Learning; they need a decision they can make, a concrete artifact they can inspect, and a way to know whether problem framed with the right feedback signal, and catch the failure where the team uses reinforcement learning where a labeled classifier would be simpler.

modules.title: Labels, structure, and rewards define the problem
modules.sub: The feedback signal chooses the learning paradigm.
modules.summary: Supervised, unsupervised, and RL differ mainly in what feedback trains them.

blocks.title: Ask what feedback exists before asking which algorithm

spans.text: Problem anchor: a product team has three ideas. Predict churn from labeled historical outcomes. Group unlabeled support tickets into themes. Teach a pricing agent to choose discounts from delayed revenue outcomes. These are different learning problems because the feedback differs: labels, hidden structure, and rewards.

blocks.analogy: The feedback signal is the teacher: answer key, pattern hunt, or reward scoreboard.

cells.text: predict churn from past churn labels

blocks.title: Feedback signal
blocks.prompt: Which paradigm fits labeled spam/not-spam emails?

options.text: Reinforcement learning because the model takes an action.

blocks.explanation: Known target labels make it supervised.

modules.title: Supervised learning predicts known targets
modules.sub: The dataset contains examples with desired answers.
modules.summary: Supervised learning fits a mapping from inputs to labels or numeric targets.
objectives: Recognize label leakage and label quality issues.

blocks.title: Supervised learning has an answer key

spans.text: In supervised learning, each training example has input features and a target: spam/not spam, churn/no churn, price, rating, or next token. The model learns a mapping that should generalize to new examples. Classification predicts categories; regression predicts numbers.

Dataset row: account_age=400 days, failed_payments=2, support_tickets=4, churned=true. The supervised task is to predict churned for future accounts. Evaluation might use recall for high-risk customers, precision for outreach cost, and calibration for probability quality.

modules.title: Unsupervised learning discovers structure
modules.sub: There is no answer key, so interpretation matters.
modules.summary: Unsupervised methods cluster, compress, visualize, or detect anomalies.
objectives: Explain clustering and dimensionality reduction as unlabeled exploration.
Connect unsupervised work to downstream decisions.

blocks.title: Unsupervised learning gives candidates, not labels from heaven

spans.text: Without labels, the model can still find patterns: nearby embeddings, dense groups, principal components, unusual points. But the output needs interpretation. A cluster may be a real product theme, a language split, a data artifact, or a scaling mistake.

The team clusters ticket embeddings and samples each group. One cluster is clearly password resets; another mixes billing and cancellation because both mention "charge." The first can become a routing candidate; the second needs better representation or more labels.

modules.title: Reinforcement learning learns from actions and delayed rewards
modules.sub: The learner changes the situation by acting in it.
modules.summary: RL is for sequential decisions where actions influence future feedback.
objectives: Explain agent, action, state, reward, and policy.
Recognize why RL is risky for many product tasks.

blocks.title: RL is about trial, consequence, and policy improvement

spans.text: OpenAI Spinning Up frames RL around agents learning by trial and error from reward or punishment. In product terms, an agent chooses an action, observes outcome, receives reward, and updates a policy. This is powerful when actions affect future states, but expensive and risky when real users carry the cost of exploration.

blocks.title: Tiny bandit update for discount choices
blocks.code:
values = {"no_discount": 0.0, "small_discount": 0.0}
counts = {"no_discount": 0, "small_discount": 0}

# Logged outcomes from a safe experiment: action, reward
history = [
    ("no_discount", 0.0),
    ("small_discount", 1.0),
    ("small_discount", 0.0),
]

for action, reward in history:
    counts[action] += 1
    # incremental average reward for each action
    values[action] += (reward - values[action]) / counts[action]

print(values)
print("current best", max(values, key=values.get))

spans.text: This is a tiny bandit-style update, not full RL. It shows the reward-feedback idea without pretending sequential product RL is easy.

predictThenReveal.prompt: Predict the average value for small_discount after rewards 1.0 and 0.0.
predictThenReveal.answer: small_discount has value 0.5. The current best is small_discount because no_discount has only reward 0.0 in this tiny history.

modules.title: Choose the paradigm by feedback, risk, and evaluation
modules.sub: The simplest viable learning setup is often the best first experiment.
modules.summary: Paradigm choice should follow data, action risk, and measurable success.
objectives: Use a decision matrix to choose a learning paradigm.
Name failure modes for each paradigm.
Plan a baseline before complex systems.

blocks.title: The paradigm is a contract with your feedback loop

spans.text: If you have clean labels, supervised learning is usually the first baseline. If you have unlabeled data and need understanding, unsupervised exploration is appropriate. If decisions affect future states and reward is measurable, RL may fit, but offline evaluation, safety constraints, and exploration risk become central.

blocks.ruleOfThumb: Choose the learning paradigm that matches the feedback you can safely and honestly measure.
blocks.useWhen: Use supervised for labeled prediction, unsupervised for exploration or compression, and RL for sequential action problems with reward and safety controls.
blocks.avoidWhen: Avoid RL for static prediction, clustering for known labels, or supervised metrics for unlabeled discovery.

blocks.title: Paradigm choice
blocks.prompt: A system must choose daily inventory orders and today's choice affects tomorrow's stockout risk. Which paradigm may be relevant?

options.text: Reinforcement learning or contextual bandits, if rewards and safety constraints are well defined.
A supervised classifier with no action feedback.

blocks.explanation: Sequential decisions with delayed rewards are the RL-shaped case.
